## Thesis

Thesis (Ph.D.)--University of Florida, 2006.

## Abstract

The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a novel, non-invasive, and non-pharmacological intervention, the use of a transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) device, on the cognitive performance of individuals with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). The study was conducted in a single-subject, multiple-baseline design across participants. The participants were recruited from a local hospital and were diagnosed with mTBI. The participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: a tDCS group and a sham group. The tDCS group received a 20-minute session of tDCS, while the sham group received a 20-minute session of sham tDCS. The participants were tested on a battery of cognitive tests before and after each session. The results of the study showed that the tDCS group had a significant improvement in cognitive performance on the cognitive tests, while the sham group did not. The results of this study suggest that tDCS may be a promising intervention for individuals with mTBI.

## Abstract

The thesis is divided into two parts. The first part is devoted to the study of the asymptotic behavior of the solutions of the following nonlinear parabolic equation:

$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\Delta u+f(u)$

in a bounded domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb{R}^N$ with $N\geq 2$ and with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We prove that the solutions of this equation converge to a solution of the following equation:

$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\Delta u+f(u)-f'(u)u$

in the sense of distributions. The second part is devoted to the study of the asymptotic behavior of the solutions of the following nonlinear parabolic equation:

$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\Delta u+f(u)+g(u)$

in a bounded domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb{R}^N$ with $N\geq 2$ and with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We prove that the solutions of this equation converge to a solution of the following equation:

$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=\Delta u+f(u)+g(u)-g'(u)u$

in the sense of distributions.

Nonlinear parabolic equation; Asymptotic behavior; Distributional solution

### Abstract

The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a brief mindfulness meditation intervention on the mood of college students. The study was conducted in a university setting with a sample of college students (N = 40). The participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: a mindfulness meditation group or a control group. The mindfulness meditation group participated in a brief mindfulness meditation intervention, while the control group did not. The intervention consisted of a brief mindfulness meditation exercise that was designed to be completed in approximately 10 minutes. The intervention was administered to the mindfulness meditation group once a week for four weeks. The participants completed a pre-test and post-test survey that included the Profile of Mood States (POMS) and the Profile of Emotional States (PES). The POMS and PES were used to measure the participants' mood. The results of the study indicated that the mindfulness meditation group experienced a significant decrease in the negative mood states of anger, depression, and fatigue, and a significant increase in the positive mood states of vigor and alertness. The control group did not experience any significant changes in their mood. The results of this study suggest that a brief mindfulness meditation intervention may be effective in reducing negative mood states and increasing positive mood states.
